articles.content:
OpenAI uses layered monitoring to detect frontier model misalignment and unauthorized agent behavior so responders can intervene before incidents escalate.

OpenAI shares model results on the Kakeya conjecture, Exponential Time Hypothesis, and quantum chromodynamics—and how researchers can verify and build on them.

We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, the latest model in the GPT-6 series. GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast, efficient model for high-volume professional work, with strong image analysis and computer use capabilities. This system card addendum provides updates on the baseline safety metrics and evaluation results for GPT-6.1 Terra.

Bringing fast and capable computer use to everyone

OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.

See how OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to uncover promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells.

Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.

GPT‑6 is rolling out globally in ChatGPT with Intelligent UI, delivering faster responses with visuals and interactive experiences you can explore and use directly.

We’re launching GPT-6 to everyone in ChatGPT, across free and paid plans globally.

articles.title: Security
articles.content:
October 29, 2026

As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.

While we’ve beenmonitoring our internal coding agentsfor some time, theHugging Face incidentexposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to theincreasing capabilitiesof our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.

In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.

In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way toreach the internet⁠(opens in a new window)from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.

While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy ofdefense in depthagainst harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controlslimit the systems an agent can access or affect; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe thatall model developersshould monitor the behavior of their most capable models.

Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used. A version of this system also monitors external tool use for models above the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities under ourPreparedness Framework, as described below in this post.

In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

Our initial layer (L0) uses lightweight classifiers we callactivation probes. They look for concerning patterns in the model’s internal activations, and pass flagged cases to the next layer for review. We tune these probes for high recall, accepting some false alarms to reduce the chance of missing concerning behavior.

Because we’re still evaluating how well the probes detect unfamiliar forms of misalignment, we also send the next layer a random 5 percent of the traffic that our probes don’t flag. Reviewing that sample helps us identify concerning behavior the probes may have missed. Because of their sensitivity, we have our frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic skip this layer and proceed directly to the next one.

At the next layer (L1), a model-based reviewer examines the agent’s recent conversation, chain of thought, and tool use. It looks for signs of deception, unauthorized actions, and attempts to manipulate an evaluation. The reviewer does this using the same context window the agent had when it acted. If the agent’s earlier work has been summarized for the context window under review, the reviewer sees that summary.

For frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic, we run an L1 check at the end of each turn and whenever the agent summarizes its earlier work to make room in its context window. We are now moving to a schedule with no more than 30 minutes between these checks.

An agent’s actions can look quite different once we know what it was asked to do. When the L1 reviewer flags a case, it’s sent to our next layer (L2) for further inspection by our investigative agent. This investigative agent can check the purpose of an evaluation and, where the full transcript is available, read back across all of the agent’s context windows to see how it arrived at its actions. The investigative agent can also write and run code in an isolated environment to examine the relevant evidence. It then uses what it finds to reconstruct the incident, identify duplicate reports, and make a decision about how serious the case is.

We use different investigative agents for different purposes. Oursecurity investigator looks for signs that someone may need to intervene—such as when an agent escaped its sandbox or accessed a system without authorization. Our alignment investigator, meanwhile, looks for behavior worth studying even when it poses no immediate security risk. Where both investigators are in use, each reviews every case flagged by our L1 layer. We are currently expanding the use of alignment investigations across our internal workloads.

For sensitive workloads, including internal Codex use, evaluations, and RL runs, a further check at our next layer (L3) draws on evidence outside the conversation. The security investigator compares the transcript with network logs, other system telemetry, and evidence from earlier cases to decide whether to alert a human responder. At L3, alignment reviewers also compare reports across cases to identify serious failures and recurring patterns, and examine frontier RL runs in greater depth.

For workloads that skip this layer, the L2 security investigator can alert responders directly.

When paging is enabled, the highest-priority security alerts reach members of our security and training teams, typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert. Responders review the evidence, examine the affected systems, and take action to contain the incident. How we follow up on less urgent findings, such as alignment failures that don’t pose immediate security risks, depends on the relevant workload.

False alarms have made it difficult to keep paging enabled around the clock for every workload. For frontier RL runs, a highest-priority alert can page a human responder at any hour. For most other traffic, we limit paging to business hours. Paging is currently disabled for internal Codex traffic. To limit potential harm while an alert is under review, some critical alerts can automatically pause the affected workload without waiting for a responder to act. We’re working toward a broader safeguard that would pause affected activity if responders have not ruled out a highest-priority alert within 30 minutes of being paged.

During the Hugging Face incident, we quarantined the internal model prototype, encrypted its weights, and restricted access to them. We also paused all relevant workloads while we introduced additional safeguards. We’re now exploring how to make these steps a standard part of our response, so that our teams can take the appropriate actions in another severe incident.

Our monitors look for both security failures that may require urgent intervention and incidents of misalignment that warrant investigation and research. Notably, our monitors were able to flag a model’s attempt toaccess the live internet using DNS⁠(opens in a new window)during an RL run within 15 minutes, with a human beginning review three minutes later.

Our publishedmisalignment reports⁠(opens in a new window)describe other incidents caught by our monitoring system. In one case, an agentexploited a testing tool to recover⁠(opens in a new window)source code that the task had deliberately withheld. The tool revealed the code in its error messages, and the agent used that code in its solution. In another, agents searching for missing task dataturned a shared software repository into a message board⁠(opens in a new window)across separate training samples.

Investigating these cases allows us to find vulnerabilities to patch, isolation boundaries to strengthen, or behaviors to address in our alignment training and evaluations. Comparing different cases that our monitors catch also helps us study how behavior changes during training, and which situations are most likely to elicit it.

articles.title: Safety
articles.content:
October 29, 2026

As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.

Today we’re updating theModel Spec⁠(opens in a new window), our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values:faithfulness to human intent,harm minimization,honesty and transparency,human agency, andcare. This reflects an aim of our work onvalue alignment: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in ourwork to refine the Specthrough research, experience deploying models,public feedbackon the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

Faithfulness to human intentis the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models shouldexpand people’s ability to shape their own livesby helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

Minimizing harmmeans respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.

Honesty and transparencymean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.

Facilitating human agencymeansstrengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.

Caremeans attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.

The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do theright thingsfor the right reasons. We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up tolasting benefits for people and society⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.

The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (seeearly work⁠(opens in a new window)and alater overview⁠(opens in a new window)). The section incorporates an updatedchain of command⁠(opens in a new window), which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection,consider context carefully⁠(opens in a new window), explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.

We’ve also added defaults onsupporting human agency⁠(opens in a new window)andfollowing relevant social norms⁠(opens in a new window), and expanded existing guidance oncontrolling and communicating side effects⁠(opens in a new window). These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.

At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences. The Spec retains stronger defaults, such asapproaching questions objectively⁠(opens in a new window). Users and developers can explicitly ask the model to take a particular perspective, but the model should not infer that preference merely from what it thinks they want to hear.

Finally, reflecting the increasing breadth of our models’ use cases and deployment settings, we now refer to the model as “GPT” rather than “the assistant” in the Spec.

This update is a first step in making the values and reasoning behind the Spec more explicit as models become more capable. The Model Spec describes the behavior we are working toward; our models do not yet fully reflect it. We will keep improving both the Spec and the models as we learn from research, real-world use, and feedback.

We want to hear which parts of the Spec you find compelling, where you disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear. Feedback on the values, trade-offs, and specific language can help us improve it. We invite you to read theupdated Model Spec⁠(opens in a new window)andshare your perspective⁠(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Prime Intellect Releases Prime Mega MoE: Trainable Fused MoE Kernel, 3.11x Faster Forward Pass
articles.content: Prime Intellect has released Prime Mega MoE, a training extension of DeepSeek’s fused Mega MoE kernel. DeepSeek’s kernel only ran the forward pass. Prime Intellect added a fast, overlapping backward pass. That makes the fused kernel usable for training, not just inference. In its prime-rl trainer, full training steps on Qwen3 MoE models run up to 34% faster. Against TorchTitan, the gain reaches 55%. For teams training mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, that is a direct cut in GPU hours. TL;DR Size: A GPU kernel, not a model. Tested on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-235B-A22B (128 experts, top-8 routing). Runs on: NVIDIA Hopper (blockwise FP8) and Blackwell (MXFP8) GPUs, BF16 on both. Published numbers use 8×H200 nodes, 32 to 128 GPUs. Performance: 32% to 34% faster full training steps than the prime-rl baseline. 48% to 55% faster than TorchTitan. Best: 3.11x faster forward pass on a Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE layer (12.0 ms to 3.9 ms). Worst: 1.24x backward pass on a Qwen3-235B-A22B MoE layer (30.5 ms to 24.6 ms). What is Prime Mega MoE? Prime Mega MoE is a fused, overlapping MoE kernel for training from Prime Intellect. It builds on the Mega MoE kernel in DeepSeek’s open-source DeepGEMM library. Why is MoE training communication-bound? In an MoE model, each token goes to a small subset of experts. Those experts sit on different GPUs. So every layer sends tokens out, runs expert math, and sends results back. This happens in the forward pass and again in the backward pass. In a standard setup, these are separate operations. The GPU sorts tokens and waits on the transport layer. Then it computes, hands results back, and waits again. Those waits are idle GPU time. How does the fused kernel work? DeepSeek’s Mega MoE, added to DeepGEMM in April 2026, replaces that chain with one kernel call. It fuses expert-parallel dispatch, the 2 expert linear layers, SwiGLU, and combine. While one token group is in transit, the kernel computes on a group that already arrived. It also skips intermediate tensors by using GPU-only scratch buffers. But it only shipped a forward implementation. Prime Intellect wrote the missing backward kernel, also overlapping. Supported types are BF16, MXFP8 (Blackwell only) and blockwise FP8 (Hopper only). The prime-rl config also exposes an fp8_bwd mode: BF16 forward, FP8 backward. &&&& How fast is Prime Mega MoE? All numbers below are self-reported by Prime Intellect. Training steps use 8×H200 nodes, FP8, 16,384-token sequences and full activation checkpointing. Each result is the mean of steps 6 to 20. Full training step, seconds (lower is better): Model (cluster)prime-rl baselineTorchTitan (FP8)Prime Mega MoEGain vs baselineGain vs TorchTitanQwen3-30B-A3B (32 H200)2.783.072.0834%48%Qwen3-235B-A22B (128 H200)12.7214.989.6532%55% Against TorchTitan, throughput rose from 5,337 to 7,886 tokens/s/GPU on the 30B model. On the 235B model, it rose from 1,094 to 1,697. The prime-rl baseline uses torch all-to-all plus DeepGEMM FP8 experts. Single MoE layer, milliseconds (1 node, 8×H200, EP=8, 128 experts, top-8, random routing): LayerForwardBackwardFull layer (2x fwd + bwd)Qwen3-30B-A3B12.0 to 3.9 (3.11x)15.4 to 8.2 (1.87x)39.3 to 15.9 (2.47x)Qwen3-235B-A22B20.7 to 9.5 (2.17x)30.5 to 24.6 (1.24x)71.9 to 43.7 (1.64x) The pattern is clear. Forward gains are large, and backward gains are smaller. The headline “up to 3.11x” refers to the forward pass only. How does it compare with other fused MoE options? FeaturePrime Mega MoEDeepGEMM Mega MoETorchTitan + DeepEPAMD Primus MegaMoEDeveloperPrime IntellectDeepSeekPyTorch, NebiusAMDTraining (backward)Yes, fused and overlappingNo, forward onlyYes (separate dispatch kernels)Yes, per design docsCompute and comms fusedYesYesNoYes (dispatch+GEMM1, GEMM2+combine)GPUsHopper, BlackwellSM90, SM100 (library)B200 in published runsMI355X (gfx950)Data typesBF16, MXFP8, blockwise FP8FP8xFP8, FP8xFP4BF16, MXFP8 grouped GEMMsBF16, MXFP8Published speedupUp to 55% step time vs TorchTitanNot disclosedUp to 41% on DeepSeek-V3 671BNot disclosedLicenseApache 2.0 (prime-rl)MITBSD-3-ClauseMIT TorchTitan’s 41% gain comes from a different setup (B200, 671B model, BF16 baseline). It is not directly comparable. How do developers use it? Prime Mega MoE is a dispatch backend in prime-rl. Set type = "mega_moe" under [trainer.model.moe.dispatch]. Choose precision from bf16, mxfp8, fp8 or fp8_bwd. The training kernels ship in a prebuilt DeepGEMM wheel from prime-kernels. The stock DeepGEMM build lacks them. Key Takeaways Prime Mega MoE adds a fused, overlapping backward pass to DeepSeek’s Mega MoE. Full training steps run 32% to 34% faster than the prime-rl baseline. Against TorchTitan, steps run 48% to 55% faster on Qwen3 MoE models. Forward gains reach 3.11x, but backward gains drop to 1.24x on large layers. It ships in prime-rl as the mega_moe dispatch backend. Check out the Prime Mega MoE blog post, the announcement on X, and the prime-rl repo. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. articles.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: An Open 30B MoE Model for 40-Language Transcription with ~4B Active Parameters
articles.content: NVIDIA has released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weights speech LLM built for transcription. One model handles 40 languages and recordings up to 1 hour. A text instruction picks the output style for each request. Options include verbatim, written form, speaker-attributed, contextual and translated output. For developers, it can replace separate ASR, diarization and alignment tools. TL;DR Size: 34B total and about 4.3B active parameters; 65,536-token context; audio up to 1 hour. Runs on: 1x H100 80 GB in BF16. FP8 (about 35 GB) and NVFP4 (about 21 GB) checkpoints exist; NVFP4 runs on an RTX 5090. GGUF files target NeMo-Speech.cpp. Performance: Best open-weights model on the English and multilingual Open ASR Leaderboards; top commercial APIs still lead. Best: 4.71% mean WER on the 9 public English Open ASR sets (next open model: 4.94%). Worst: 34.95% cpCER on AliMeeting Mandarin far-field meetings. Bottom line: Best thing: 1 open model covers transcripts, speaker labels, timestamps and translation. Worst thing: offline only, with weak Mandarin meeting accuracy. What is Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe? Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a speech-augmented language model (SALM) from NVIDIA that turns audio and instructions into text. An audio encoder feeds embeddings into an LLM decoder, which makes transcription promptable. NVIDIA’s technical research report argues there is no single correct transcript. Numbers, fillers and domain terms depend on who reads the output. NVIDIA positions the model as a transcription specialist, not a general-purpose assistant. How does the architecture work? It has three parts: Parallel Expert Encoder: a trainable 0.6B Transformer ASR encoder runs beside a frozen Nemotron 3 Diarization model. The diarizer tracks up to 8 speakers. Its speaker activity is added to the ASR features every 80 ms. The LLM therefore sees who spoke when, without architecture changes. LLM backbone: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE. It has 52 layers: 23 Mamba-2, 23 MoE and only 6 attention layers. Each MoE layer routes to 6 of 128 experts plus 1 shared expert. Few attention layers keep the KV cache small for hour-long audio. Add-ons: a shared multi-token prediction (MTP) layer drafts tokens for speculative decoding. A 50M-parameter CTC adapter aligns the finished transcript to audio for word timestamps. The model name says 30B-A4B, but the checkpoint holds about 34B parameters. The extra weight comes from the 1.3B MTP module and the audio components. articles.title: Baseten Releases joey-1, a 2B Decision Model at $0.01 per 1M Tokens
articles.content: Baseten has released joey-1, a 2B model from its in-house research lab, Base Labs. The joey-1 decision model returns a label and a calibrated probability instead of generated text. It targets high-volume routing, classification and guardrail checks. Baseten prices it at $0.01 per million input tokens, with open weights on Hugging Face under MIT. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, post-trained from Qwen3.5-2B. 16,384-token max sequence (Baseten says 262k on dedicated deployments). Runs on: Baseten Model APIs, or self-hosted on 1 CUDA GPU (VRAM not disclosed). No official quantized builds listed. Performance: Top model under 4B on the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, per Baseten. Best: 63.30 on Jev Decision Index 0.4 (public split), ranked #37 of 230 models. Worst: Trails its 9B sibling elephant-1 by 8.94 points on the same split (63.30 vs 72.24). Bottom line: Best: 20 ms P50 decisions for $0.01 per 1M tokens. Worst: less general knowledge than its larger siblings. What is joey-1? joey-1 is a 2B decision model from Baseten’s Base Labs that answers typed questions in 1 forward pass. You send a state (text or images) and 1 or more questions. The model returns a probability for every option of every question. It does not write free-form text that your application must parse. It supports 3 question types: choice: pick 1 named option, such as which team owns a ticket. yes/no (noul in the API): returns the probability of yes. score: ordered levels, lowest first, such as urgency. joey-1 is the third member of a family. Baseten shipped mammoth-1 (27B) and elephant-1 (9B) last week. All 3 share training data and the /v1/systemone API, so switching is a 1-line change. How does joey-1 work? Base Labs post-trained Qwen3.5-2B with a full fine-tune of the language model. The vision encoder stays frozen. Full-attention layers use a block-bidirectional mask. All questions are answered from 1 shared-prefix prefill, so extra questions add little cost. Training details from the model card: Data: 6.21M decision examples. Mix: 58.3% core decision skills, 16.1% safety, 16.1% judging and expert domains, 9.5% public data. Objective: cross-entropy plus a Brier calibration term, with a trained “I don’t know” option. Recipe: 1 epoch, 43,390 steps, peak learning rate 1e-5, bf16. Hardware: 2 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. Calibration lets you set a confidence threshold. Uncertain answers can escalate to elephant-1, mammoth-1 or a human. && How fast and cheap is joey-1? Baseten reports a P50 end-to-end latency of 20 ms for an average 2,000-token request. That is about 2.5x faster than elephant-1 (49 ms). The blog’s TL;DR also claims 5x faster than comparable decision models, without naming them. Model APIs charge $0.01 per 1M input tokens; output and cached input are listed at $0.00. elephant-1 costs $0.035 and mammoth-1 costs $0.10. Baseten’s example: 10M support tickets a month at about 500 tokens each is 5B tokens. That is about $50 on joey-1, versus $500 on mammoth-1. How does joey-1 score on benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported on Baseten’s model card. On the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, joey-1 scores 63.30. That ranks #37 of 230 models and is the top score under 4B. The Jev Decision Index is a community leaderboard on Hugging Face. On the same split, Cloudflare’s 27B Clef scores 61.71 and Jev 1.14 scores 60.70. joey-1 trails elephant-1 in every area. It beats Jev 1.14 in 4 of 5 areas, including language, tools and retrieval. On Baseten’s replica of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, joey-1 scores 62.9, versus 65.9 for mammoth-1. joey-1 vs. other small decision models Featurejoey-1elephant-1Perplexity Decider Flash v1.2Cloudflare Clef-FlashDeveloperBaseten (Base Labs)Baseten (Base Labs)PerplexityCloudflareParameters2B9B4B9BBase modelQwen3.5-2BQwen3.5-9BQwen3.5-4BQwen3.5-9BLicenseMITMITApache-2.0Apache-2.0InputsText, imagesText, imagesText, imagesText, JSON, images, videoMax context16,384 (Model APIs); 262k on dedicated16k (Model APIs); 262k on dedicated262,144 (trained to about 32k)16,384 defaultAPI price per 1M input tokens$0.01$0.035$0.01Not disclosedJev Decision Index 0.4 (public)*63.3072.2460.06Not disclosedReported latency**20 ms P5049 ms P50Not disclosed38.8 ms medianSelf-host hardware1 CUDA GPUNot disclosedAbout 9 GiB BF16 weights on a CUDA GPUTested on 1 H200Weights accessPublicPublicPrivate repo, token requiredPublic *Jev 0.4 scores for all models come from Baseten’s joey-1 model card. **Latency figures are not comparable. Baseten measures end-to-end on its platform; Cloudflare reports its own Decision Index 0.2.1 run. How do you deploy joey-1? Model APIs: call decision-models/baseten-joey-2b-latest at /v1/systemone. Zero data retention is on by default. Dedicated deployments: Baseten says these unlock 262k context, fine-tuned weights and co-location with LLM workloads. Self-hosted: download from Hugging Face and run setup.sh. It needs 1 CUDA GPU and a PyTorch 2.8 / CUDA 12.8 image. You can fine-tune joey-1 on Baseten Training Jobs using the fine-tuning cookbook. joey-1 is also listed on OpenRouter at $0.01 per 1M input tokens. Key Takeaways joey-1 returns labels plus calibrated probabilities, not text. Baseten reports 20 ms P50 latency at $0.01 per 1M input tokens. 63.30 on Jev Decision Index 0.4 public: top model under 4B. Trails elephant-1 by 8.94 points; best as a first-line router. MIT weights on Hugging Face; self-host on 1 CUDA GPU. Check out the blog post, model card, model library page and fine-tuning cookbook. articles.title: Infini-AI-Lab Releases Hermit, an Open-Source Harness Adapter Framework for AI Agents
articles.content: Infini-AI-Lab has released Hermit, an open-source harness adapter framework for AI agents. Hermit is a framework from Infini-AI-Lab that trains an external ‘harness adapter’ while the agent’s model and harness stay frozen. The first release, v0.1.0, shipped on October 25, 2026. CMU postdoc Haizhong Zheng announced it on X on October 27. For developers, the pitch is simple: adapt Codex or Claude Code agents to new tasks without fine-tuning or forking the harness. TL;DR Footprint: A Python framework. No parameters of its own. Apache-2.0, pip install hermit-harness. Runs on: The offline Quick Start needs no GPU, model account or dataset. Real runs use any API backend or a local vLLM, SGLang or Ollama server. Performance: Reported gains over no-adapter baselines on OfficeQA, CL-Bench and ServeLearnBench, all with GLM 5.3 Flash. Best: MWM adapter hits 0.795 accuracy on CL-Bench database exploration, vs 0.580 for the in-context baseline. Worst: The prompt-only adapter scores 0.470 on the same venue, below that 0.580 baseline. Bottom line: Best: one training loop for 5 harness evolution methods. Worst: most results are single runs, self-reported. What is a harness adapter? A harness adapter is a trainable external harness. It works like a plugin with training support built in. A model adapter, such as LoRA, adapts a model. A harness adapter adapts an existing agent instead. The adapter can hold instructions, skills, memory, tools, executable code and agent coordination logic. It can even be a whole repository. Its specification says which parts are learnable and how updates get checked. The base model and harness never change. The team gives 3 reasons for this design. Many harnesses are closed-source. Editing open ones can break carefully tuned component interactions. And a learned adapter can move between compatible models and harnesses. How does Hermit train an adapter? Hermit uses an RL-style training loop. A Trainer runs a batch of tasks through the acting agent with the current adapter. A judge scores the outputs. An Evolver reads the trajectories and feedback, then proposes a new adapter. The Trainer checks it against the template and commits it as the next version. Every adapter version lives in a git tree. You can inspect, roll back or ship any version. Learner programs can run sandboxed, which requires Linux with bubblewrap. Five evolution methods ship today: GEPA, SkillOpt, MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness² and Continual Harness. ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon. You can also write your own Evolver. articles.title: Block Unveils Dessa, a Full-Duplex Speech Model Trained Only on Speech
articles.content: Block’s AI research lab has released Dessa, a full-duplex speech model trained only on human conversation. Block announced it on October 23, 2026 as a research preview. Dessa is a speech-to-speech model from Block that listens and talks at the same time. Block says it used no text and no pretrained models. That is a different design from the text-first stacks behind most voice agents today. TL;DR Runs on: A MacBook Pro M4 Max or better, locally, faster than real time. Performance: Demo-only so far. Live recordings show backchannels, mid-sentence laughs and natural interruptions. Best: Trained on 1 NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack (72 GPUs). Moshi used 1,016 H100 GPUs. Worst: 0 published benchmark scores. No weights, paper, API or price. What is Block’s Dessa? Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model: audio in, audio out. According to Block’s project page, everything it knows came from human speech. It is full-duplex, so it listens while it talks. Block says it learned from real conversation when to cut in. It also learned when to backchannel with short cues like “yeah” or “got it”. Block’s demo clips show Dessa laughing mid-sentence and getting louder when asked to speak up. One clip shows it talking with OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1. Block says nobody steered any clip. How does speech-only training work? Most voice systems chain 3 parts: speech recognition, a text model, then speech synthesis. Block team argues that chain throws away emotion, sarcasm, laughter and sighs. Dessa hears and produces those signals directly. Block has not published the architecture. Here is what it has disclosed: Training data: human conversation audio only. No text and no pretrained models. Compute: 1 NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, which links 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs. Data efficiency: Block says Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words than LLMs need. Inference: faster than real time, on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better. The lab also explains why this is hard. Speech never repeats exactly. A spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text. Kyutai’s Moshi, the best-known open full-duplex model, takes another route. Moshi starts from a text language model backbone and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Its model card lists 7 million hours of pretraining audio and 1,016 H100 GPUs. & How does Dessa compare with Moshi, PersonaPlex and GPT-Live-1? articles.title: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
articles.content: AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1, its first text-to-speech model, now generally available. The AssemblyAI-TTS-1 text-to-speech API targets voice agents running on live phone calls. In that setting, latency and pronunciation decide whether a caller stays on the line. Pricing is $15 per 1M characters, with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to buy. For developers already using AssemblyAI speech-to-text, it closes the voice loop with one vendor. TL;DR Size: It is a hosted API model. Runs on: AssemblyAI’s cloud only, in the US (us-east-1) or EU (eu-north-1). No open weights or on-prem option. Any client with HTTP or WebSocket works. Performance: Ties ElevenLabs v4 on entity accuracy in AssemblyAI’s tests, at under 1/5 of its price. Best: 47 ms median time to first byte across 6 models in AssemblyAI’s API test (self-reported). Worst: 159 ms median streaming latency on Cekura’s independent benchmark, 8th of 19 timed models. Bottom line: Best: $15 per 1M characters with unlimited concurrency. Worst: no SSML, speed control, pronunciation dictionaries or emotion tags yet. What is AssemblyAI-TTS-1? AssemblyAI-TTS-1 is a streaming text-to-speech model from AssemblyAI that turns agent replies into speech for live calls. It was trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data. Most TTS models represent audio as discrete tokens. AssemblyAI says TTS-1 operates on continuous audio representations instead. The AssemblyAI claims this improves realism and cuts time to first spoken audio. The launch includes a library of 4,000+ voices and instant voice cloning. A clone needs a short recording and a confirmation of the speaker’s permission. The clone in the launch post used 24 seconds of audio. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese. How do developers integrate AssemblyAI-TTS-1? There are 3 interfaces: an HTTP API, a WebSocket API and an OpenAI-compatible route. The WebSocket session keeps one connection per conversation and accepts a cancel message for barge-in. Output is mono PCM, mu-law or A-law, at 8 kHz to 48 kHz. 24 kHz PCM is the native format; telephony stacks can request 8 kHz mu-law directly. Word timestamps are included. AssemblyAI also published LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents. How does AssemblyAI-TTS-1 perform on benchmarks? AssemblyAI tested TTS-1 against 5 models on 4 English sets, using 50 matched cloned voices. All figures below are self-reported, from an eval dated October 28, 2026. Entity accuracy (580 hard targets such as phone numbers and codes): 93.7%, vs ElevenLabs v4 93.6%, Cartesia Sonic 3.6 82.5%, ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 68.0%. Word accuracy: 99.0% on Seed-TTS and LibriSpeech sentences. Predicted MOS: 3.85, behind Inworld TTS-2 Flash at 3.88 and ahead of Sonic 3.6 at 3.82. Median time to first byte: 47 ms. Flash v2.5 took 119 ms, Sonic 3.6 143 ms, Inworld TTS-2 Flash 244 ms. Other: 85.5 TTSDS prosody score and 0.64 speaker similarity for cloned audio. Independent results are more mixed. On Cekura’s benchmark of 27 models, TTS-1 scored 81.5% reading accuracy and 4.50 naturalness. Its median streaming latency, timed from the last word sent, was 159 ms. Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% accuracy there, at the same $15 price. AssemblyAI also cites a 1.7% word error rate on Coval’s leaderboard. It reports a top-10 debut in Artificial Analysis’ controlled-voice arena. articles.title: 의료 AI 판단 오류 줄인다…앤테리어, 임상 기준 검증 가능한 규칙으로 바꾸는 오픈소스 공개
articles.content:
의료 인공지능(AI)이 동일한 환자 기록을 분석하고도 서로 다른 판단을 내리거나 복잡한 임상 기준을 누락하는 문제를 줄이기 위한 새로운 기술이 공개됐다. 대형언어모델(LLM)이 의료기록을 분석하되, 최종적인 기준 적용은 사전에 검증된 규칙에 따라 수행하도록 분리한 것이 핵심이다.

미국 의료 AI 기업 앤테리어(Anterior)는임상 정책의 적용 일관성을 높이고 AI 판단 과정을 추적·검증할 수 있도록 설계한 오픈소스 프레임워크 '심볼릭 리즈닝(symbolic-reasoning)'을 9일(현지시간) 공개했다.

이번 기술은 기호 추론 그래프(Symbolic Reasoning Graphs, SRGs)를 기반으로 한다. 복잡한 임상 지침과 보험 심사 기준을 구조화된 실행 규칙으로 변환하고, 의료 전문가가 해당 규칙을 사전에 검토·검증할 수 있도록 설계됐다.

기존 LLM 중심의 의료 AI는 방대한 진료기록을 읽고 필요한 정보를 추출하는 데 강점이 있지만, 같은 임상 기준을 사례마다 다르게 해석하거나 일부 요건을 빠뜨릴 가능성이 있다. 이러한 불일치는 의료 서비스 지연이나 행정 업무 증가, 부정확한 보험급여 판단으로 이어질 수 있다.

앤테리어는 이를 해결하기 위해 AI의 정보 분석 기능과 규칙 적용 기능을 분리했다. 먼저 AI 모델이 환자의 진료기록을 분석해 특정 임상 요건이 충족됐는지 확인한다. 이후 규칙 기반 시스템이 미리 정의된 정책 논리를 적용해 판단 결과를 도출한다. 이 과정에서 어떤 기준을 검토했고 각 항목을 어떻게 판단했는지 기록으로 남긴다.

예를 들어 특정 치료에 대한 보험 사전승인(Prior Authorization)을 심사할 경우 AI는 환자의 진단 내용과 검사 결과, 치료 이력을 분석한다. 이후 해당 치료에 필요한 임상 기준을 충족했는지는 사전에 검증된 규칙에 따라 평가하는 방식이다.

이러한 구조는 AI가 임상 정책 전체를 매번 새롭게 해석하는 방식과 달리, 동일한 기준을 반복적으로 적용할 수 있도록 지원한다. 의료진 역시 판단 근거를 세부 항목별로 확인하고 오류 여부를 검토할 수 있다.

앤테리어는 수천 건의 의료 관련 정책을 다루면서 축적한 경험을 바탕으로 이 기술을 개발했다. 적용 대상으로는 진료 사전승인뿐 아니라 의료서비스 품질 평가, 보험 청구 및 급여 확인, 지급 적정성 검토 등이 제시됐다.

이번에 연구용 프리뷰로 공개된 오픈소스에는 기호 추론 라이브러리와 복잡한 정책을 표현하는 전용 언어 '에스알지 랭(srg-lang)', AI 시스템과 외부 도구의 연동을 지원하는 모델 컨텍스트 프로토콜(Model Context Protocol, MCP) 서버가 포함됐다.

아누즈 이라바네(Anuj Iravane) 앤테리어 AI 책임자는 "의료 AI가 불필요한 행정 업무를 줄이려면 시스템이 어떤 과정을 거쳐 결론에 도달했는지 신뢰할 수 있어야 한다"고 강조했다.

이어 임상 지침을 적용하는 데 필요한 의료진의 전문지식을 명시적인 규칙으로 표현함으로써 AI가 동일한 기준을 일관되게 적용하고 판단 근거를 제시하도록 설계했다고 설명했다.

앤테리어는 이 기술을 의료 분야뿐 아니라 복잡한 규정 준수와 판단 근거의 입증이 필요한 금융·법률 분야에도 적용할 수 있을 것으로 보고 있다.

이번 발표는 의료 AI의 신뢰성을 높이기 위해 언어모델의 성능 개선에만 의존하지 않고, 전문가가 검증한 규칙과 AI의 정보 분석 기능을 결합하려는 접근이라는 점에서 주목된다. 특히 의료기록을 해석하는 과정과 임상 정책을 적용하는 과정을 구분하면 판단 근거를 검토하기 쉬워지고, 의료진의 감독을 유지하면서 행정 자동화를 확대할 수 있다.

다만 이번 공개는 연구용 프리뷰(다운)단계로, 실제 의료기관과 보험 심사 환경에서 판단 오류가 얼마나 감소하는지에 대한 정량적 검증 결과는 제시되지 않았다. 향후 임상 정책의 정확한 규칙화와 의료기록 분석의 신뢰성, 전문가 검토체계가 기술의 실질적인 활용 수준을 결정할 것으로 보인다.

한편, 미국 뉴욕에 본사를 둔 앤테리어(Anterior)는 의사 출신 압델 마흐무드(Abdel Mahmoud)가 설립한 의료 AI 기업으로, 건강보험사의 진료 사전승인 심사와 의료기록 검토, 보험급여 관리 등 복잡한 의료 행정 업무를 자동화하는 기술을 개발하고 있다. 세쿼이아 캐피털과 NEA 등으로부터 투자를 유치했으며, 2026년 2월 기준 누적 투자금은 6400만 달러에 달한다.
articles.summary: 앤테리어는 LLM의 의료기록 분석과 검증된 임상 규칙의 적용을 분리하는 오픈소스 프레임워크를 연구용 프리뷰로 공개했다. 기호 추론 그래프로 임상 지침과 보험 심사 기준을 실행 규칙으로 표현하고, 전문가가 사전 검토하며 판단 근거를 항목별로 추적하도록 설계했다. 공개 구성에는 기호 추론 라이브러리, 전용 언어 srg-lang과 MCP 서버가 포함돼 사전승인·급여 확인 등의 업무 통합을 지원한다. 다만 실제 의료·보험 환경에서 오류가 얼마나 감소하는지에 대한 정량 검증은 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $\pi$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $\pi$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 RAG에서 검색 문맥과 모델 내부 지식이 충돌할 때 어느 한쪽을 고정적으로 우선하는 규칙에는 한계가 있다고 분석한다. 두 출처 각각의 증거와 문맥이 맞을 사전확률을 결합해 답하거나 응답을 유보하는 방법을 제안한다. GRACE에서 올바른 문맥의 실제 비율을 사전확률로 제공했을 때 모든 혼합 비율에서 최선의 기준선을 웃돌았으며, 최대 격차는 26점이었다. 다만 모델 자체에 관련 지식이 없으면 이득이 사라졌고, 운영 환경에서는 문맥 신뢰도에 대한 적절한 사전확률을 확보하는 문제가 남는다.

articles.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36355v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
articles.summary: WAKMan은 실시간 요청 패턴에 맞춰 프리픽스 KV 캐시의 퇴거 정책을 선택하는 관리자다. 연구는 짧은 간격으로 돌아오는 에이전트 요청에는 최근성 중심 정책이, 인기 프롬프트나 긴 대화에는 빈도 중심 정책이 유리하며 20개 트래픽 혼합에서 항상 최선인 단일 정책은 없었다고 보고한다. WAKMan은 프롬프트를 읽거나 요청 유형을 미리 알지 않고 정책을 선택해 LRU 대비 캐시 적중률을 평균 5%포인트 높였다. 혼합형 LLM 서비스의 프리필 계산 절감 가능성을 보여주지만, 실제 비용이나 지연 감소 수치는 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.
articles.summary: CohortFlow는 임상 코호트 선정 기준의 수정 사항을 구조화된 명세와 지속적인 실행 그래프에 국소적으로 반영하는 에이전트다. 의미적 의존관계를 기록해 바뀐 기준과 관련된 계산만 다시 수행하며, 100개 시나리오 평가에서 수정 지연을 완료 후 64.8%, 실행 중 44.3% 줄이고 모델 호출을 38.1% 줄였다. 요구사항 micro-F1은 77.0%로 전체 재생성의 76.4%와 통계적으로 유의한 차이가 없어, 핵심 성과는 정확도 향상보다 재계산 비용 절감이다. MIMIC 개념검증에서는 13개 코호트 상태가 모두 실행됐지만, 이를 광범위한 임상 검증으로 보기는 어렵다.

articles.title: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GPU clusters have become essential computing resources for AI and scientific research in academia and industry. However, their high cost and growing demand often result in long queueing delays. While previous monitoring efforts have operated at second- or minute-level frequencies, they primarily informed job-level scheduling for clusters and lacked the detail needed to optimize GPU-level utilization.
  This paper presents an in-depth study of a university research GPU cluster, analyzing resource usage at 100 ms intervals. We have developed a lightweight monitoring tool that leverages Nvidia's DCGM library to capture fine-grained "compute utilization" metrics within GPUs. Deployed on a cluster with 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, our tool collected data over several months. This paper focuses on a 10-day period with 7,399 jobs submitted by 150 users from 12 departments. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) the GPU cluster exhibits significant underutilization, with over 70% of jobs using less than 20% of GPU memory and 50% averaging below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization; (2) 80% of jobs have a drastic mismatch between their requested and actual durations, significantly limiting the scheduler's effectiveness; and (3) the multi-GPU jobs we examined show highly periodic communication patterns. These findings suggest there is plenty of room in the middle: substantial utilization gains are available through better job scheduling and GPU multitasking, independent of hardware or application improvements.
  Our monitoring solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/als244/gpu_server_monitoring.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 NVIDIA DCGM 기반 도구로 대학 연구용 GPU 클러스터를 100밀리초 간격으로 관측해 자원 활용의 빈틈을 분석했다. 319개 GPU를 갖춘 클러스터의 10일간 7,399개 작업에서 70% 이상은 GPU 메모리 사용률이 20% 미만이었고, 절반은 평균 SM 활용률이 5% 미만이었다. 작업의 80%에서 요청 시간과 실제 실행 시간의 큰 불일치도 관찰돼 스케줄링과 GPU 다중 작업 개선 가능성을 제시한다. 모니터링 도구는 오픈소스로 제공되지만, 단일 대학 클러스터의 수치를 모든 AI 인프라로 일반화해서는 안 된다.

articles.title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.
articles.summary: StruPO는 이미지 생성 프롬프트를 개선하면서 사용자가 요청한 객체 속성과 관계를 보존하도록 학습한 편집 정책이다. 보정된 장면 그래프와 이미지 기반 보상을 활용하고, 여러 생성 결과를 평균해 이미지 생성의 확률적 변동을 다룬다. 세 개의 독립적인 2천 프롬프트 시험 세트와 네 개의 고정 생성 모델에서 충실도와 미적 품질의 균형이 개선됐으며, 자동 평가와 15명 평가자의 선호 조사에서도 근거를 제시했다. 그래프 보정 후 반복적인 비평·재작성 없이 한 번에 편집문을 만들 수 있어 프롬프트 최적화 과정의 단순화 가능성이 있다.

articles.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.36308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 에이전트 메모리에서 최신 사실을 검색했더라도 오래된 상충 정보가 함께 있으면 답변 정확도가 떨어질 수 있음을 보여준다. MemoryAgentBench의 단일 홉 과제에서 Qwen2.5-7B는 검색 증거를 64토큰에서 512토큰으로 늘리자 정확도가 45%에서 32%로 하락했으며, 사후 감사에서는 모든 검색 결과에 최신 진술이 포함돼 있었다. 증거 길이를 고정한 통제 실험에서도 무관한 문장을 오래된 경쟁 진술로 바꾸면 정확도가 크게 낮아졌다. 특정 과제와 모델의 결과라는 한계는 있지만, 메모리 시스템에서는 검색량 확대보다 사실의 최신성 관리와 충돌 해소가 중요할 수 있다.
